For instance, hybrid systems (e.g. biogas micro-CHP) to co-produce heat and power are being explored to further enhance resiliency in winter. Conceptually, these microgrids can be scaled from single buildings to networks of resilience hubs, however determining siting, financing, and resilience value of this approach is often beyond the capacity of smaller municipalities. A resilience hub is a trusted local facility (school, church, community center) augmented with solar and storage and other systems so it remains a safe, warm/cooled gathering place during outages. Technical analyses (e.g. using NREL’s REopt tool) find that solar PV drastically cuts operating costs and batteries ensure multi-day backup power for these hubs (Menghaney 2025). Case studies show community service providers (e.g. clinics, shelters) are highly motivated by energy resilience often ranking “ability to operate during outages” as their top goal, even above cost savings (Ramanan 2022). 6 This highlights that resilience-minded organizations prioritize backup power as a critical service during disasters. Despite enthusiasm, small local governments face hurdles in turning plans into projects. Limited staff and technical expertise mean many municipalities are unfamiliar with emerging storage technology and lack energy usage data and permitting know-how (Ramanan 2022). A Clean Energy Group survey noted that community organizations often “struggle with limited staff time and resources,” making lengthy solar and storage projects daunting. Financially, thin budgets make it hard to cover even the soft costs of development, placing the higher cost, lower return option of storage generally off the table even for discussion. Policy uncertainty (fluctuating incentives, complex utility tariffs, interconnection rules) further complicates planning in most communities. Utilities generally possess the most capacity and technical expertise to pursue solar, solar and storage, and microgrids, however there has been limited success in obtaining regulatory approval (Kallay 2021). because such proposals often fail to align with traditional regulatory objectives. The primary obstacle for utilities is the difficulty in securing funding, as utility regulators are rarely approving ratepayer investments in microgrids, leading to mixed success in regulatory proceedings thus far. Regulator resistance is largely due to the inability to quantify resilience benefits or resilience benefits that do not show utility-system cost- effectiveness. Approval instead has frequently hinged on utilities demonstrating blue sky financial benefits that may not be competitive with returns on other utility investments. According to Sandia National Laboratories’ The Quest for Public Purpose Microgrids for Resilience: Considerations for Regulatory Approval (Kallay 2021), utility proposals often lack alignment with traditional utility system needs, with many projects not being sited or scaled to maximize benefits like avoiding or deferring other utility investments. Finally, projects are typically one-time, single microgrid efforts, rather than strategically planned portfolios, which regulators find insufficient for comprehensively adding resilience to the overall utility system. Challenges of proving cost effectiveness and resilience value faced by utilities are similar to challenges that municipal employees may face in determining appropriate resilient energy approaches at a smaller scale.
